newsitem.title: USA: Mazda looks for U.S. comeback with new 626, pickup.
newsitem.headline: Mazda looks for U.S. comeback with new 626, pickup.

text.p: Mazda Motor Corp. unveiled new versions of its 626 sedan and compact pickup truck Thursday, touting the vehicles as the beginning of a comeback for the Japanese automaker in the United States.
The 1998 626 is due out in October, company officials said at the car's introduction at the New York International Auto Show. The 626 is Mazda's highest volume vehicle in the United States.

The car was exclusively designed for the North American market and will only be sold here. It is longer and wider than the previous car for a smoother ride, and features a stiffer body for improved handling.
Interior room and trunk volume also have been increased. The engine comes in two more powerful versions, a 2.0-liter four cylinder and a 2.5-liter V-6.

Mazda's new B-Series compact pickup, based on the Ranger from Ford Motor Co., was redesigned to give it a more sporty, rugged look. Mazda also boosted the interior room, upgraded the ride and handling and installed a more powerful base engine.

"With the introduction of these two core, volume products, Mazda is embarking on a renewal and revitalization of the franchise," said George McCabe, general manager of Mazda Motor of America, the North American unit of Mazda Motor Corp.
He added the automaker, which is one-third owned by Ford, plans to introduce at least one new model a year through 2000.
Mazda can use it. Sales are plunging at a time when other Japanese companies are experiencing huge growth.

Mazda's sales were down nearly 17 percent in the first two months of 1997 to 28,718. For all of 1996, they were off 16 percent to 238,265. By contrast, Toyota Motor Corp. sales have shot up more than 30 percent so far this year.

But sales will not being going up any time soon. McCabe said the 626 production changeover at its Auto Alliance joint venture in Flat Rock, Mich., will hold back sales this year. He expects both sales and U.S. market share, which stands at 1.6 percent, to be flat this year compared with 1996.

When the 626 reaches full volume production, the company expects to make about 85,000 a year. Annual B-Series production at Ford's Edison, N.J., plant is expected to be 50,000 to 60,000 units. Neither vehicle has been priced yet.

Richard Beattie, who joined Mazda Motor of America as chief executive earlier this month, told reporters Thursday he was drawing up plans for a major efficiency restructuring at all of Mazda's North American operations. That may include staff cuts among the 1,600 workers Mazda has in the United States and Canada, although no cutbacks are currently planned.
"There are no sacred cows," he said.
Beattie said his plans also call for increasing Mazda's U.S. market share to 2 percent, perhaps by sometime in 1998.
In addition to the 626 and B-Series, Mazda Thursday showed a concept of its Protege sedan with safety and personalized features tailored specifically for women.

Designed with input from "New Woman" magazine, the car has an indirect lighting system that enables the driver to clearly see the back seat and not be spotlighted as they enter the vehicle. The keyless entry device is tied to a global positioning system to help police locate the vehicle.
